946.title: Paris, 1893
946.hook: he dies in a Paris hotel, far from home
946.howItsDone: Duleep Singh is buried at Elveden in Suffolk, and Sikh visitors to the churchyard remember him there; some Sikhs hold prayers for him and his mother at gatherings about the end of the kingdom.

segments.voice: Yesterday, amrit, and your line was he came back. Today, the end of the road for the man who came back.

A hotel room in Paris. Outside, the boulevards, the cafés, the noise of a great city. Inside, a man lies weak after a stroke, his body failing. He was born in Lahore. He sat on a throne as a child, lost it, grew up in a garden by the Ganges, lived as a gentleman in Suffolk, and came back to Sikhi in a port at Aden. Now he is here, in a rented room in a city that was never his home.
screen: `A HOTEL ROOM IN PARIS.` → `A MAN WEAK AFTER A STROKE.` → `A CITY THAT WAS NEVER HOME.`

segments.voice: After Aden, Duleep Singh could not go to India and would not go back to his old life in England. He went to Paris. He tried to win support abroad for his claim to the Punjab, and even traveled to Russia hoping for help. None came. His money ran low, his first wife died, and his health broke. Late in life, weakened, he wrote to Queen Victoria asking her pardon, and she forgave him. They met once more: the Queen who held his diamond, and the Maharaja who had once fought her government with words. He died in a hotel in Paris, far from the Punjab and far from Elveden. His body was taken back to England and buried in the churchyard at Elveden, beside his wife and son, with a Christian service. He had come back to Sikhi, but he was not cremated with Sikh rites. For some who tell his story, that is one more thing taken from him. In a hymn of Guru Arjan, the Guru says that since he found the company of the holy, he has forgotten all envy of others; no one is his enemy and no one is a stranger, and he gets along with everyone. An exile is someone everywhere treats as a stranger. The Guru's line describes a company where nobody is one. So today's line reaches past Duleep Singh, to everyone far from home.

You don't need faces or names; just hold them all in your mind for a while, without judging how they got there. If you pray, you can hold them before God, and say Waheguru.

947.title: Princess Sophia, suffragette
947.hook: Duleep's daughter Sophia campaigned for women's votes in Britain
947.howItsDone: Sikhs in Britain remember Princess Sophia Duleep Singh as a suffragette, and her story is often told alongside the Gurus' teaching that women and men are equal in the sangat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paris, where Duleep Singh died far from Punjab, and your line was for all exiles. Today, one of the children he left behind.

Outside the gates of Hampton Court Palace, near London, a woman in a fine coat holds up a newspaper for sale. It's called The Suffragette. People walking past might know her face. She lives just across the road, in a grace-and-favor house the old Queen herself granted her. She is a goddaughter of Queen Victoria. Her father was the last Maharaja of the Sikh kingdom, the boy who lost a crown. And here she is on the pavement, selling a paper that demands the vote for women.
screen: `A PRINCESS SELLING A NEWSPAPER.` → `A GODDAUGHTER OF THE QUEEN.` → `THE DAUGHTER OF DULEEP SINGH.`

segments.voice: Sophia Duleep Singh grew up English in every outward way: country houses, ponies, dresses, and later a grace-and-favor home at Hampton Court. She could have stayed there quietly, and nobody would have blinked. As her biographer Anita Anand tells it, a journey to India changed her. She saw Punjab, the land her father had ruled, and people living under a government they had no voice in. Back in Britain, women had no vote either. She joined the women fighting for one, the suffragettes, and she didn't do it from the back row. She walked with the women who went to Parliament to demand the vote, on a day when the crowd was met with force. She refused to pay her taxes, saying in effect: no vote, no tax. So officials seized her things, jewelry among them, and sold them at auction, and the fight went on. Guru Nanak, in the Asa di Var, asks why anyone would speak ill of woman, when it is from woman that kings themselves are born. Sophia was raised far from the Gurus' hymns, and nobody can say how much of them she knew. But a daughter of the Sikh royal house stood in the street for women's equal voice, and the old line and the new march sound alike.

948.title: Princess Bamba
948.hook: another daughter moved to Lahore and kept the family's memory
948.howItsDone: Visitors to the Lahore Fort can see the Princess Bamba Collection of Sikh-era paintings and objects, and some Sikh families keep their own memory of the Sikh kingdom in pictures, stories and visits to Lahore.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Princess Sophia at the palace gates, and your line was the princess marched. Today, her older sister, who went the other way: east.

A house in Lahore, full of old things. Paintings of men in turbans and jewels. Small portraits on ivory. Pieces of a vanished court, gathered one by one and kept in a city this family once ruled. The woman who gathered them was born in England, raised English, and could have stayed there all her life. Instead she moved to Lahore, the capital her grandfather Ranjit Singh had ruled, and her father had lost as a boy.
screen: `A HOUSE FULL OF OLD PORTRAITS.` → `BORN IN ENGLAND.` → `SHE MOVED TO LAHORE.`

segments.voice: Bamba Duleep Singh was Duleep Singh's eldest daughter, Sophia's sister. Like Sophia, she grew up in English houses, far from Punjab, with a father who had been taken from it. She traveled to Punjab, and in the end she stayed. She married a doctor who taught at the medical college in Lahore, and made her home in the old capital. For a child of an exiled family, that was a quiet kind of return: not to a throne, but to a street, a house, a city. Over the years she gathered what she could of her family's past: paintings, portraits, objects from Ranjit Singh's court. After she died, the collection passed into the care of the government in Lahore. Today it is known by her name, the Princess Bamba Collection, held at the Lahore Fort. A kingdom was gone, its rooms had emptied, and one granddaughter set about gathering up what was left. The Gurus use the word simran for remembering: holding the Name of God in mind, again and again, so it isn't lost. What Bamba did is not simran in that sense; her remembering was of a family and a court. But the two share a shape: memory doesn't simply stay. Somebody keeps it, or it goes. Bamba died in Lahore and is buried there, in the city her family once ruled.

949.title: Sikh soldiers under the Raj
949.hook: after the great rising against Company rule, the British recruited Sikhs heavily into the army
949.howItsDone: Sikh regiments have kept the Guru Granth Sahib with them, read by a regimental granthi, and Sikh families remember soldier ancestors who served overseas in the British Indian Army.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Princess Bamba in Lahore, and your line was she kept the memory. Today we leave the royal family and follow ordinary Sikh men into uniform.

A barracks at dawn, a very long way from Punjab: a hot port, a cold frontier, a city where nobody speaks Punjabi. Rows of young men tie their turbans before parade. In one room, set apart, a granthi opens the Guru Granth Sahib and reads the morning's hymn. These soldiers wear the uniform of the British Crown. Not long before, men from the same villages had fought the British at Ferozeshah and Sobraon.
screen: `TURBANS TIED BEFORE PARADE.` → `THE GURU IN THE BARRACKS.` → `ONCE ENEMIES, NOW RECRUITS.`

segments.voice: After the wars and the annexation, the British army in India was shaken by a great rising against Company rule. Punjab did not join it in strength, and Sikh soldiers fought on the British side. After that, the British looked to Punjab for soldiers, and Sikhs were recruited heavily. British officers came to call Sikhs a martial race, a label about whole peoples that historians now treat with care. And the army wanted its Sikh soldiers to look like Khalsa Sikhs: uncut hair, the turban, the outward form. Some histories argue that this helped keep the Khalsa form strong in villages at a time when it might have faded. The Guru went too. Sikh regiments carried the Guru Granth Sahib with them, with a granthi to read it, so a soldier posted far from home could still hear the hymns in the morning. Service took these men to garrisons and battlefields across the empire, far from wives, parents and fields. In a hymn of Guru Ram Das in Raag Asa, the Guru says that wherever the true Guru goes and sits, that place is made beautiful. A barracks room far from Punjab, with the Guru Granth Sahib open in it, could be read that way. But the uniform belonged to a foreign Crown, and Sikhs still talk about what that meant: honor, a living for poor families, and a hard question about whose battles they were fighting.

950.title: Canal colonies
950.hook: new canals turned dry land green and Sikh farmers moved west to farm it
950.howItsDone: Sikh families from the old canal colonies of western Punjab still tell stories of the villages their grandparents built there, and Sikhs who recite the Japji in the morning end it with the salok that names water as the father.

segments.voice: Yesterday, granthi, and your line was far-off service. Today, the men who stayed with the land, and a land that changed under them.

Dry ground, cracked and pale, with thorny scrub and not much else. Herders cross it with their animals. Rain is rare. Then a channel of water arrives, cut straight across the plain, and the ground on either side darkens. Within a few seasons there is wheat where there was dust, and a family from a crowded village in central Punjab is standing in a field that, a few years before, was nobody's farm at all.
screen: `DRY GROUND AND THORNY SCRUB.` → `A CHANNEL OF WATER ARRIVES.` → `WHEAT WHERE THERE WAS DUST.`

segments.voice: In western Punjab, between the rivers, lay wide dry uplands that people called the bar. British engineers dug canals from the rivers across this land, and where the water went, farms could grow. The government granted the new land to families brought in from other parts of Punjab. Sikh farmers were among them, leaving crowded home villages for bigger plots out west. They built houses, wells and gurdwaras, and whole new villages grew up around the canals. New market towns were laid out to serve the colonies. One of them, Lyallpur, was planned with bazaars running out from a clock tower at its center. Today that city lies in Pakistan, and how Sikh families left these lands is a later, harder story. For now, it was a story of water and wheat. The salok at the close of the Japji names the world as a family: air is the Guru, water is the father, and the great earth is the mother. In the colonies, farmers could watch that line take shape, water making fields out of dust. No crop grew on that plain until the water came, and a farmer's whole year hung on the canal running on time.

951.title: Missionaries and debates
951.hook: Christian missions and new Hindu reform groups debated with Sikhs over identity
951.howItsDone: Sikh histories describe the late nineteenth century as a time of public debate in Punjab, when Sikhs founded presses, newspapers and societies to explain their faith; Sikhs read Guru Nanak's Sidh Gosht as a model of question and answer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the canal colonies, and your line was water made fields. Today, Punjab gets noisy: preachers, presses and arguments.

A crowded bazaar in a Punjab town. On a wooden platform, a preacher is speaking about his faith, and a small crowd has gathered. Across the street, a printing press turns out pamphlets in Punjabi and Urdu, some arguing with the preacher, some arguing with each other. In a schoolroom nearby, a teacher is telling Sikh boys a story about who their Gurus were, and it isn't the story their grandmothers told. Everybody has an answer to the same question: what are the Sikhs?
screen: `A PREACHER IN THE BAZAAR.` → `PRESSES TURNING OUT PAMPHLETS.` → `WHAT ARE THE SIKHS?`

segments.voice: With British rule came Christian missionaries. They opened schools and hospitals, printed books, and preached in towns and bazaars. Some Sikhs studied in their schools, a few became Christians, and each conversion was felt in the wider community. In the same years a Hindu reform movement, the Arya Samaj, grew strong in Punjab, calling people back to the Vedas and opening schools of its own. Some of its writing spoke harshly of the Sikh Gurus, and Sikh writers answered that it struck at who they were. Punjab filled with public meetings, newspapers and pamphlets. Christians, Arya Samajis, Muslims, Sikhs: each wrote, each answered, and the arguments could be sharp. Sikhs set up presses and societies to answer in print, and to teach their own history in their own words. Guru Nanak had faced hard questions too. In the Sidh Gosht, the Guru Granth Sahib records a long conversation with the yogis: they ask, he answers, they ask again, and the whole thing moves by question and reply rather than shouting. And in another hymn Guru Nanak says that, as long as we live in this world, we should listen to some and say some. In the Guru's line, the listening comes before the saying.

952.title: The keepers of the gurdwaras
952.hook: hereditary keepers treated gurdwaras as private property
952.howItsDone: Sikh histories remember the era of the mahants as the background to the gurdwara reform movement, and they also honor the Udasi custodians who kept gurdwaras open in hard times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gosht, and your line was calm in debate. Today ends a week that ran from Paris to Punjab's own gurdwaras.

A gurdwara door, and a man with the keys. He didn't build the gurdwara, and the sangat didn't choose him. He holds the keys because his teacher held them before him, and his teacher's teacher before that. The offerings that pilgrims leave go into his keeping. The land around the shrine is written in his name. If the sangat doesn't like how he runs it, there isn't much they can do. His title: mahant.
screen: `A MAN WITH THE KEYS.` → `HANDED DOWN, NOT CHOSEN.` → `MAHANT.`

segments.voice: A mahant is the head of a religious house, a title used beyond the Sikh tradition too. Sikh histories say that in hard years, when Khalsa Sikhs were hunted and often far from home, gurdwaras were looked after by custodians, among them Udasis, an order of ascetics who honor Guru Nanak. Thanks to them, doors stayed open. Over time the keeping passed from teacher to chosen disciple, or father to son. Under British rule the courts tended to treat the shrine and its land as the mahant's own property. What had been a trust began to look like an estate. Some mahants, not all, lived well on the offerings and ran the gurdwaras as they pleased. Reformers complained of practices in some shrines that they said went against the Gurus' teaching, and of a sangat with no say over its own house of worship. Guru Nanak says that taking what rightly belongs to another is as forbidden as the food a person's own faith forbids. A gurdwara belongs to the sangat. When one man holds it as his own, something shared has slipped into private hands. Looking back on this week: an exile dying in Paris, a princess marching, a princess keeping memory, soldiers far away, farmers on new land, Punjab arguing with itself, and now the keys of the gurdwaras in a few private hands. A people without a kingdom, asking what was still theirs.
